learn.title: Insert without moving data
learn.body: With an array, inserting in the middle shifts many items. A list only changes pointers. Find the node to insert after, then wire the new node in with two assignments.

learn.title: Insert after a node
learn.body: Link the new node forward first, then link the earlier node to it.

learn.title: Order of the two lines
learn.body: `n->next = p->next` saves the rest of the list. Only then is it safe to change `p->next`. In the other order, p->next would already point at n, and the old rest of the list would be lost.

learn.title: Inserting 2
learn.body: The list is 1, then 3. Call `insert_after` on the node holding 1.
steps: A new node holds 2, with next not yet set
`p->next = n` points node 1 at the new node

learn.body: To insert at the very front there is no node before it, so the head pointer itself must change.

questions.prompt: Why is inserting into a list in the middle cheap?
choices: Only pointers change, no items shift
questions.explanation: Existing nodes stay where they are in memory.
First save the rest of the list in the new node. Then link the earlier node.

questions.prompt: The list is 5, 9. You call `insert_after` on the node holding 5 with value 7. What is the list's second value?
Insert a node at the front by making its next the old head, then moving \_\_.
questions.explanation: The head pointer must now point at the new first node.

questions.prompt: What would `p->next = n` first, then `n->next = p->next` do?
questions.explanation: After the first line p->next is n, so the second line sets n->next to n. The old rest is lost.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to insert after node p.
questions.explanation: Set the new node's next first, then link p.
